views.name: city_core
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city.city_name AS city_name,
  city.population AS population,
  city.state_name AS state_name,
  city.country_name AS country_name
FROM city

params.description: Provides one-row-per-city basic demographic attributes (population and the city's state and country names).
params.when_to_use: Find or list cities and their population (e.g., "largest cities in Wyoming"). | List cities together with their state_name and country_name attributes. | Filter, group, or aggregate at the city_name grain (city-level summaries such as total population by state when aggregating city rows). | Enrich another one-row-per-city dataset by joining on city_name when that other dataset is also guaranteed one-row-per-city.
params.output_schema: city_name: city_name from city — city identifier string (view grain) | population: population from city — per-city population value (numeric) | state_name: state_name from city — the state name associated with the city | country_name: country_name from city — the country name associated with the city
params.metric: population = city.population
params.composition: Safe to join to another table that is one-row-per-city on city_name (e.g., JOIN other_table ON city_core.city_name = other_table.city_name) because city_core is one-row-per-city. | If joining to a table that has multiple rows per city_name (the many side), first aggregate that table to city_name (e.g., SELECT city_name, SUM(amount) FROM transactions GROUP BY city_name) then join to city_core to avoid duplicating city-level population. | If you need aggregates at a higher grain (state or country), aggregate population after selecting from city_core (e.g., SELECT state_name, SUM(population) FROM city_core GROUP BY state_name).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when the question requires a different grain than city_name (for example, neighborhood-level, multiple records per city, or person/transaction-level detail) because this view is explicitly one-row-per-city and lacks lower-level identifiers. | Do not join directly to a many-side table keyed by city_name (e.g., transactions, events) without first aggregating the many-side to city_name — doing so will multiply city-level attributes such as population and produce incorrect results. The SQL exposes population as a per-city value, so joining to multi-row-per-city data without aggregation changes intended semantics. | Do not use when city identity is ambiguous or when the dataset contains multiple city records per city_name (alternate identifiers) — the view selects only columns from the base city table and assumes city_name identifies a single row; if your data model has multiple rows per city_name you must disambiguate by additional keys before reusing this view.
params.dialect_notes: Dialect: SQLite — SQL uses simple SELECT ... FROM city with no dialect-specific functions; no windowing or complex joins present.

params.output_schema: state_name: state.state_name (state name, one row per state) | population: state.population (state.population as stored in state table) | area: state.area (state.area from state table) | density: state.density (state.density from state table) | capital: state.capital (state.capital from state table) | country_name: state.country_name (state.country_name from state table)

params.composition: Cardinality-safe: join to country- or state-level dimension/views on country_name or state_name (e.g., country_dim.country_name = state_core.country_name or state_dim.state_name = state_core.state_name) — safe because state_core is one-row-per-state. | Unsafe: do NOT join state_core directly to one-to-many child tables (e.g., city tables) on state_name without aggregating the child first (for example: SELECT state_name, COUNT(*) AS city_count FROM city GROUP BY state_name) to avoid multiplying state-level attributes.
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use this view to answer questions that require lower-grain details (e.g., city-level lists, city counts, or other per-city measures) without joining or aggregating appropriate child tables — the view is one-row-per-state and contains no city rows. | Do not join this view directly to one-to-many child tables (such as city-level tables) without first aggregating the child side to one row per state; otherwise you will duplicate state-level measures (population, area, density) because state_core is already at state grain.
params.dialect_notes: Dialect: SQLite — SQL uses simple SELECT FROM state with column aliases; no dialect-specific functions are present.

views.name: cities_by_state_ranked
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.city_name AS city_name,
  c.state_name AS state_name,
  c.population AS population,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY c.state_name ORDER BY c.population DESC) AS population_rank_in_state
FROM city_core c

params.description: For each city (one row per city_name): its state, population, and the city's dense population rank within its state (1 = highest population).
params.when_to_use: Find the city or cities in a given state with the highest population (e.g., "which city in Wyoming has the highest population?"). | Label or filter city-level rows by their within-state population rank (for example: WHERE population_rank_in_state = 1). | Present city-level lists grouped by state while keeping each city's population and its rank within that state.
params.output_schema: city_name: city name (from city_core.city_name) | state_name: state name (from city_core.state_name) | population: population (from city_core.population) | population_rank_in_state: dense rank within state partition ordered by population DESC (computed)
params.metric: population_rank_in_state = DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY city_core.state_name ORDER BY city_core.population DESC)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE: join to state-level one-row-per-state tables on state_name (state_name = cities_by_state_ranked.state_name) without duplicating city rows, because the view is one row per city_name. | cardinality-SAFE: join to one-row-per-city dimensions on city_name — preserves city-level grain and does not duplicate population or rank. | unsafe-to-join without aggregation: do NOT join to tables that are one-to-many from city (e.g., city_events) without first aggregating those child rows to city_name — such joins will multiply city rows and thus distort population and rank. | recompute-on-grain-change: if you aggregate this view up to state or another grain, recompute ranks at the new grain rather than relying on population_rank_in_state (it is only meaningful per city within state as computed).
params.when_not_to_use: Do not use when the analysis requires a different grain than one row per city_name (for example, state-level aggregates or neighborhoods) — the view is computed at the city_name grain and its rank is per city within state, so collapsing to state will make population_rank_in_state meaningless unless re-computed. | Do not use when city identity is ambiguous or when city_name is not a unique key in the dataset — the view assumes one row per city_name as the grain (if city_name duplicates exist in city_core, the rank and row-per-city assumption will be incorrect). | Do not use if you need ranks computed over a different population measure or different partitioning (e.g., national rank, metro-area rank, or rank by a different population column) — the view computes DENSE_RANK() partitioned by state_name ordered by population DESC as written.
params.dialect_notes: SQLite: uses DENSE_RANK() window function which is supported in modern SQLite versions (ensure the runtime SQLite build includes window function support).

       c.state_name,
       c.population
FROM city_core c
JOIN state_core s ON c.state_name = s.state_name

params.description: Provides one row per city (by city_name) for cities that have a non-null state and population, exposing the city's state and population.
params.when_to_use: List cities with their state and population (filtered to rows where both state and population are known). | Build aggregations by state (e.g., total or average population) using these validated city rows as a base. | Join to city-level dimensions or facts that are known to be one-row-per-city to enrich city attributes without duplicating population measures. | Serve as a clean input to ranking or windowed computations that require non-null state and population values.
params.output_schema: city_name: the city identifier/name; derived from city_core.city_name | state_name: the state's name for the city; derived from city_core.state_name (and validated by an inner join to state_core.state_name to ensure the state exists in state_core) | population: the city's population value (non-null); derived from city_core.population
params.metric: population = city_core.population (base numeric attribute, no further aggregation in this view)
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_core on state_name — safe because this view contains at most one row per city (grain = city_name) and state_core is a state-level dimension (one row per state). Joining on state_name will not duplicate this view's city-level rows or its population values. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to city_core (or other one-row-per-city views/dimensions) on city_name — safe because matching is one-to-one by city_name, so population is not duplicated. | do NOT join directly to one-to-many tables or views keyed by city_name (for example, a hypothetical city_events table with multiple event rows per city) without re-aggregating the many-side first — such a join would multiply the city rows and therefore multiply the population measure, which would incorrectly inflate aggregations that sum population. | do NOT join to sibling one-to-many analytical views (e.g., any view that ranks or lists multiple records per city) unless you first aggregate those views to one row per city (for example, count_events_by_city aggregated to city_name) or use windowed semantics that preserve the intended measure semantics. | If you need state-level aggregates (total population per state), aggregate this view by state_name (e.g., SUM(population) GROUP BY state_name) rather than joining to a state-level facts table that contains multiple city rows, to avoid double-counting. | When composing further: treat population here as a base-level city attribute. Any multi-row join that is kept must be accompanied by an appropriate GROUP BY or DISTINCT-on-city_name step to preserve the one-row-per-city grain before summation.

views.name: cities_aggregated_by_state_avg_population
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  city.state_name AS state_name,
  COUNT(*) AS city_count,
  AVG(city.population) AS avg_city_population,
  SUM(city.population) AS sum_city_population
FROM city
WHERE city.state_name IS NOT NULL
  AND city.population IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY city.state_name

params.description: Per-state aggregations of city counts and city population (average and sum) — one row per state_name.
params.when_to_use: Get number of cities, total city population, and average city population per state. | Rank or filter states by average or total city population. | Compose higher-level metrics that need per-state city aggregates as inputs (e.g., state population share from cities) while avoiding re-scanning the city table. | Join with state-level descriptive attributes (one-row-per-state) without changing the aggregated measures.
params.output_schema: state_name: The state name grouping key; derived from city.state_name in the city table (used in GROUP BY). | city_count: The count of city rows in that state included in the aggregation; derived from COUNT(*) over rows from the city table filtered by non-null state_name and population. | avg_city_population: The average population of those cities in that state; derived from AVG(city.population) over the same filtered city rows. | sum_city_population: The sum of population across those cities in that state; derived from SUM(city.population) over the same filtered city rows.
params.metric: city_count = COUNT(*)  -- count of city rows per state after WHERE filters (city.state_name IS NOT NULL AND city.population IS NOT NULL) | avg_city_population = AVG(city.population)  -- average of city.population over the counted city rows per state | sum_city_population = SUM(city.population)  -- sum of city.population over the counted city rows per state
params.composition: cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to state_core on state_core.state_name = cities_aggregated_by_state_avg_population.state_name — safe because state_core is one-row-per-state (one-to-one with this view's grain), so this view's measures are not duplicated. | cardinality-SAFE join guidance: join to cities_by_state_ranked on state_name if that sibling view is one-row-per-state (verify it is aggregated at state granularity) — safe only when that sibling also has exactly one row per state; otherwise re-aggregate after joining. | do NOT join cities_aggregated_by_state_avg_population directly to city (or any other one-to-many child of state keyed by state_name) without re-aggregation — joining to city would produce multiple city rows per state and multiply city_count / sum_city_population unless you re-aggregate (e.g., by joining on state_name and then grouping and recomputing aggregates or by joining to a deduplicated state-level table). | do NOT join to city_rows_with_valid_state_and_population or city_core if those are one-to-many (city-level) on state_name without re-aggregating first — such joins will duplicate the per-state measures. | If you need to combine this view with additional city-level filters or compute city-level derived metrics, either (a) apply those filters/derivations to the city table and build a new aggregated view, or (b) join this view to a DISTINCT state-level dimension (one row per state) and compute new metrics that do not rely on city-level detail, to preserve correctness.

views.name: cities_with_state_45
views.body_sql:
SELECT
  c.city_name AS city_name,
  c.population AS "city.population",
  c.state_name AS "city.state_name",
  s.population AS "state.population AS state_population",
  s.area AS "state.area AS state_area",
  s.country_name AS "state.country_name AS state_country_name"
FROM city c
LEFT JOIN state s
  ON c.state_name = s.state_name

params.description: Provides one-row-per-city with that city's population and the matching state's population, area, and country — answers questions that look up city attributes together with their state's attributes.
params.when_to_use: Lookup a city's population and its state's population/area/country by city name or by filtering on city attributes (e.g., 'What is the population of X city?' or 'Which city in Alabama has the smallest population?'). | Iterate over cities and report their city-level and matching state-level attributes in a city-grain result (one row per city). | Filter or report cities based on predicates that reference both city and state attributes (e.g., cities where state.area > X) when you expect one output row per city.
params.output_schema: city_name: city.city_name (city name, one row per city) | city.population: city.population (population of the city) | city.state_name: city.state_name (the state's name as stored on the city row) | state.population AS state_population: s.population (state population copied onto the city row) | state.area AS state_area: s.area (state area copied onto the city row) | state.country_name AS state_country_name: s.country_name (state's country name copied onto the city row)
params.grounded_columns: city.city_name | city.population | city.state_name | state.population | state.area | state.country_name | state.state_name
params.metric: city.population = city.population (base city-level measure; do not aggregate this view's state_population when computing state totals) | state_population = state.population (state-level attribute repeated per city row; treat as dimension, not a rollup-safe metric)
params.composition: This view is one-row-per-city (grain = city.city_name). Join cardinality guidance: | - Safe: join this view to one-row-per-state dimensions (for example the base table state keyed by state_name) to attach additional state-level attributes — doing so should not duplicate city rows. | - Unsafe: do NOT join this view directly to one-to-many tables keyed by city_name (e.g., transactions, events) without aggregating the many side to one row per city first, because that will multiply city rows and duplicate city.population. | - Unsafe: do NOT rely on summing state_population from this view to compute state totals; instead use SUM(city.population) GROUP BY city.state_name or take state.population from a true one-row-per-state source. | - Explicit assumption: the view assumes state.state_name is unique in the state table; if state has multiple rows per state_name, state attributes will be duplicated across city rows.
params.when_not_to_use: Computing state-level aggregates by summing state_population from this view (wrong because state_population is repeated on every city row; summing will overcount). Instead aggregate city.population (SUM(city.population) GROUP BY state_name) or obtain state population from a one-row-per-state source. | Joining this view to a one-to-many table keyed by city_name (e.g., transactions with multiple rows per city) without first aggregating the many-side — that would multiply city rows and duplicate city.population or any city-level measures. | Joining this view to a multi-row-per-state table (e.g., state_counties) without aggregating that multi-row-per-state source first, unless you intend to expand city rows by county — the LEFT JOIN in this view assumes state_name in state is unique; if state has multiple rows per state_name this view's state columns may duplicate unexpectedly.
params.dialect_notes: SQLite: the SQL uses SQLite-compatible syntax. Note the SELECT alias for state.population is written as s.population AS state.population AS state_population in the SQL — this is syntactically incorrect in most dialects; actual intended aliases are provided in output_schema. Treat the SQL as mapping s.population -> state_population, s.area -> state_area, s.country_name -> state_country_name.
